messages.author: 2330bbb33122f310
messages.subject: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
parts:
Dear all

I am trying to convince a co-author of the excellence of INLA with regard to hypothesis testing. As a starting point I have resorted to rather simple numerical cases, but these do not come out all convincing. The general question is whether I ask for the impossible, or whether there are INLA commands unknown to me which may give me what I want.

The setting is one of grouped observations. A single grouping provide the simplest possible structure for random effects and might be convincing. Data are generated with two correlated covariates, x1 with only group level values, x2 with individual values, y = x1*a1 + x2*a2 + normal noise. The true model is easily recovered with fixed-effects INLA or OLS.

The problem is to predict the value of a1 given y, x1 and grouping only, and also of a2 given y, x2 and grouping. These settings are realistic ones since few models have all the covariates observed. 

When the number of groups is small relative to the number of observations, a fixed effect model (with Z as group matrix) may work,

(1)      y = x1*a1 + Z*b1 + noise1

(2)      y = x2*a2 + Z*b2 + noise2

Model (2) gives convincing values of a2 and its st.dev, while (1) does not with regard to a1. I presume these results are related to the fact that in (1) the grouping Z cannot carry complete information on the missing x2, while in (2) the grouping can carry information on the missing x1 (which is itself grouped).
 
Alternatively, I have tried random effects b1 and b2 with Z as effect matrix. Results are then wrong for both models. The precision of random effects becomes too high. 

Questions are then: Why does (2) work while (1) does not with fixed effects? And how should the appropriate random effect models be specified?

best
Øyvind

(test file is included)

messages.author: 2330bbb33122f310
messages.subject: Re: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
parts:
Dear all

Let me make this post simpler. In the previous version I did ask for too much. Random or fixed effects associated with group dummies will only carry information on group level. This is why the group effect in model (1) deviates from the true model, while the individual effect in model (2) coincide. 

The remaining issue is: How do I specify group effects as "fixed" and "random" so that results are equivalent?  

My "fixed" effect specification is ok for relative small numbers of groups. When group numbers are counted in hundreds or thousands, the formulas will be overly long and a "random" effect is required. In low dimensions I presume equivalent specifications exist, but I have not found them. Part of the story may be related to equivalent priors. I find INLA rather vague on this, and the celebrated PC priors are not the answer in my case.  

best
Øyvind

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
parts:
I'm not absolutely sure that I understand your question, so let me know if the answer makes sense or not.

If you have a factor variable: "group number", you can either
1) Use fixed effects (one for each factor level, where the reference level is covered by the intercept)
2) Random effect: IID replicate over the groups (determining deviation from intercept level)

When you use the fixed effects, the priors are essentially flat. This means that if you have one group without observations, you will get an almost flat posterior (sd=31) for that fixed effect.

When you use random effect, you have a pooling parameter sigma (precision^-0.5), telling you the size of the priors. If you have a group with no observations, the posterior from this will be the prior, of the size that you determined (by sigma) through fitting the other groups. 

Having the pooling parameter (1 extra hyperparameter) is generally thought to be a good idea, and the reason to use hierarchical models.

Håvards reply shows you how to make the same model in two different ways, namely by fixing the value of this pooling parameter.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
parts:
Additionally, with regards to your script (it is a bit hard to read), I note that you simulate from
>> x1 = (Z %*% rnorm(n.g))[, 1]*sd.x1

This simulates one level for each group, from the same distribution N(0, sd.x1^2). One natural way to do inference on this is to use the IID random effect (with covariate being the group number), where the precision parameter is trying to figure out what the true sd.x1^-2 is.

In this case, however, you would only supply the group identities to the data, and not x1 itself (as you did)...

Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
parts: log precision is - log(1000)
"the replication of the fixed effect results are much better than with estimated precision"

Why are they better? Better at predictions? Recover the truth inside interval?

- To me, the best model is that which you believed generated the data. Hence, if you think the group effect can be completely different, you want flat prior, but if you think they should be of the same size roughly, you want to infer parameter.
- By the way, the defualt priors are not so good. we recommend inla.doc("pc.prec"). Especially for sparse data!
"in particular with low dimensional data"

Hmm, low dimensional can mean 2 different things here
- Few groups
- Few observations per group
- Both
Which one are you talking about?
- If you have few groups, the inference about sigma/precision makes little sense, as you have no replicates to determine the size of the iid model.

On Sunday, April 23, 2017 at 12:15:53 PM UTC+2, Haakon Bakka wrote:

I'm not absolutely sure that I understand your question, so let me know if the answer makes sense or not.

If you have a factor variable: "group number", you can either
1) Use fixed effects (one for each factor level, where the reference level is covered by the intercept)
2) Random effect: IID replicate over the groups (determining deviation from intercept level)

When you use the fixed effects, the priors are essentially flat. This means that if you have one group without observations, you will get an almost flat posterior (sd=31) for that fixed effect.

When you use random effect, you have a pooling parameter sigma (precision^-0.5), telling you the size of the priors. If you have a group with no observations, the posterior from this will be the prior, of the size that you determined (by sigma) through fitting the other groups. 

Having the pooling parameter (1 extra hyperparameter) is generally thought to be a good idea, and the reason to use hierarchical models.

Håvards reply shows you how to make the same model in two different ways, namely by fixing the value of this pooling parameter.

Kind regards,

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
parts: "My real data are not that sparse. There are otherwise warnings against pc priors with hypothesis testing as far as I remember? And there are also warnings against default priors.  log precision = - log(1000) give me flat prior which is neither. My follow up is whether it should be fixed or not?"

This "sparse" depends on how many observations you have per group. I would guess that if you have like 100+ observations per group, you may as well go with flat priors, as you have enough strength in the data.

You could also consider doing model comparison between the two models (fixed precision and inferred precision), e.g. with CPO or another prediction measure. There is also the possibility to stop doing hypothesis testing altogether and just do (predictive) model comparisons instead.

PS: The flat prior is still a "default prior", just of a different kind; it will sometimes overestimate the size of the effects.

Kind regards,
Haakon
